'''III) Temple of Hatshepsut''' Because the ruin was completely buried beneath rubble in the early 19th century, travellers did not realise that another temple lay hidden beside Hatshepsut’s. In 1858 workmen under [[:en:Auguste Mariette|Auguste Mariette]] discovered a cache of 72 mummy coffins belonging to priests of [[:en:Montu|Montu]] (22nd–26th Dynasties). In 1859 [[:en:Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|Lord Dufferin]] began excavations with Dr Lorange and Cyril C. Graham, clearing the southwest corner of the hypostyle, uncovering the plundered tomb of Queen [[:en:Tem (queen)|Tem]] and proceeding toward the sanctuary, where they found a seated statue of Amun‑Re and a granite altar of Mentuhotep. Further finds followed, including the tomb of [[:en:Neferu II|Neferu]] ([[:en:TT319|TT 319]]). In 1898 [[:en:Howard Carter|Howard Carter]] discovered the Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), clearing a mock burial and recovering the celebrated black seated statue of the king. [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel im Querschnitt.JPG|thumb|left|Cross‑section by Édouard Naville]] [[File:Mentuhotep-Tempel-Plan.JPG|thumb|Plan by Édouard Naville]] From 1903 to 1907 [[:en:Édouard Naville|Édouard Naville]] excavated the site for the Egypt Exploration Fund. Although Lord Dufferin had first revealed part of the plan, Naville was the first to expose and record the entire complex.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 1, Mainz 1974, p. 70. Between 1920 and 1931 [[:en:Herbert Eustis Winlock|Herbert E. Winlock]] led five seasons for the [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]], publishing only preliminary summaries.Ibid., p. 70 f. From 1967 to 1971 [[:en:Dieter Arnold|Dieter Arnold]] cleared and re‑studied the monument for the [[:en:German Archaeological Institute|German Archaeological Institute]], publishing his results in three volumes.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. == Architecture == === Causeway and forecourt === [[File:MentuhotepII-FuneraryStatue-CloseUp MetropolitanMuseum.png|thumb|left|upright|Head from a standing statue found in the forecourt (1921/22; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] [[File:Mentuhotep Deir el-Bahri.jpg|thumb|Aerial view of the temple]] [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel Sitzstatuen im Vorhof.JPG|thumb|Remains of two seated statues of Mentuhotep II in the forecourt]] Like its Old Kingdom predecessors, the complex possessed a sunken {{ill|Ancient Egyptian Valley Temple|lt=valley temple|de|Taltempel|ja|谷神殿|zh|峡谷神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and a 1.2 km long, 46 m wide processional {{ill|Causeway (Ancient Egypt|de|Aufweg|lt=causeway|it|Rampa processionale|cs|Vzestupná cesta}}, no longer roofed. The causeway ended in a vast forecourt enclosed by cliffs and planted with rows of trees and royal statues. Archaeology has identified pits for at least 57 [[:en:Tamarix|tamarisk]] and 6 [[:en:Ficus|sycomore fig]] and beds for flowers, allowing reconstruction of a rare [[:en:Gardens of ancient Egypt|temple garden]].H. Winlock in Arnold, *The Temple of Mentuhotep …*, New York 1979, p. 21 ff.Robichon–Varille in Arnold, *ibid.*, p. 21. A team of gardeners must have maintained irrigation from the Nile a kilometre away, creating greenery amid desert. At least twenty‑two seated sandstone statues of the king flanked the causeway, apparently crowned with the [[:en:Hedjet|White Crown of Upper Egypt]] on the south and the [[:en:Deshret|Red Crown of Lower Egypt]] on the north. One such statue found by Winlock in 1921/22 is now in New York.Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010), p. 21.
=== Eastern (front) section === West of the causeway lies the actual sanctuary, designed as a terrace temple in two parts. The front section was dedicated to [[:en:Montu|Month]]‑[[:en:Ra|Ra]], a fusion of the Theban war‑god and the sun‑god. The eastern façade presents colonnades on both sides of the ramp, each of two rows of square pillars evoking a {{ill|saff tomb|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 11 ff. A central ramp (Naville’s 1905 reconstruction) leads to the upper terrace, overlaying the original ramp whose lowest limestone revetment survives in two places.Ibid., p. 16 f. [[File:MentuhotepII-Reste des Ambulatoriums.JPG|thumb|Remains of the ambulatory and a corner of the core building]] On the terrace a 60 × 43 m, 5 m‑high podium supports the upper colonnade, a triple‑aisled {{ill|ambulatory|de|Ambulatorium|ja|周歩廊|zh|回廊|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the core building. The ambulatory comprised 140 octagonal pillars enclosed by a 5‑ell thick wall, creating a covered passage round the solid core. Entrances lay on east and west. Only bases or stumps of many pillars remain.Ibid., p. 21 f. The core, cleared in 1904/05, is a solid square block 22 m per side and 11 m high. Naville and Winlock reconstructed it as surmounted by a pyramid, but Arnold rejects this on structural grounds.Ibid., p. 27 ff.Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, p. 159.M. Höveler‑Müller, *Am Anfang war Ägypten*, Darmstadt 2013, p. 142. === Western (rear) section === [[File:MentuhotepII.jpg|thumb|Painted limestone block from the relief programme (Naville 1907; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] The rear portion, serving the cult of the deified king, was partly cut into the cliff and comprised an open court, a hypostyle with statue chapel, and later, a shrine to Amun‑Re, converting the complex into a true {{ill|million‑year house|de|Millionenjahrhaus|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 141. The middle court west of the ambulatory was flanked north and south by six columns and east by a double colonnade of eight columns. At its centre a deep [[:en:Dromos|dromos]] descends to the royal tomb. Finds include a limestone altar, a granite stele and six granite statues of [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]].Ibid., p. 33. West of the middle court lies the hypostyle hall (8 × 10 columns), separated by a wall and slightly higher.Ibid., p. 34 f. The sanctuary consists of a rock‑cut {{ill|speos|de|Speos|ja|スペオス|zh|石窟神殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} with a fore‑hall. All walls bore painted raised reliefs.D. Arnold, *ibid.*, Bd. 3, p. 15. Fragments show the king receiving cult as a god among gods.Ibid., p. 16. The statue room yielded an over‑life‑size standing statue of the king and a seated image of Amun‑Re, perhaps another royal theophany.Ibid., p. 33 f. === Foundation deposits === Under the terrace corners Winlock discovered intact foundation pits containing cattle skulls, food offerings, bricks and inscribed objects.Ibid., Bd. 3, p. 49 ff. Similar deposits under the core, cleared 1970, included linen inscribed with Mentuhotep’s and [[:en:Intef II|Intef II]]’s names.Ibid., Bd. 1, p. 52 ff. === The royal tomb === From the west court a 150 m sloping corridor leads to a granite burial chamber lined with rose granite and roofed corbel‑wise. Inside stood an alabaster shrine once sealed by double doors, which contained the wooden coffin and unpreserved funerary furniture of the king.Ibid., p. 44 ff.; Kühn 2010, p. 26. === Bab el‑Hosan === [[File:Bab el-Hosan.JPG|thumb|left|Entrance to Bab el‑Hosan (2010); background: Mentuhotep and Hatshepsut temples]] The Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), north of the causeway, was accidentally discovered when Carter’s horse fell through its roof in 1898. It is a secondary royal tomb: a 40 m shaft and 150 m sloping corridor leading west to a chamber where Carter found the black seated statue of the king and a deeper pit containing three wooden boats and pottery.Ibid., p. 51 ff. Arnold interprets it as an Osiris tomb providing the king magical resurrection.Ibid., p. 82. === Tomb of Tem === In the southwest corner of the hypostyle lies the tomb of the great wife Tem, aligned parallel to the king’s tomb and containing a colossal alabaster sarcophagus and a fragmentary offering slab.Ibid., p. 53 f. === Six tombs of queens and a princess === [[File:ShrineOfKemsit.jpg|thumb|Chapel of Kemsit (drawing by Margaret Naville)]] [[File:MentuhotepII-ShrineOfSadhe-Entrance.JPG|thumb|Entrance to the chapel of Sadeh (after Margaret Naville)]] Six richly decorated chapels with underground shaft‑tombs for the wives [[:en:Ashayet|Ashayet]], [[:en:Sadeh (queen)|Sadeh]], [[:en:Kawit (queen)|Kawit]], [[:en:Kemsit|Kemsit]], [[:en:Henhenet|Henhenet]] and princess {{ill|Mayet|de|Majit|ja|マイト|zh|马伊特|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were set into the west wall of the ambulatory. Their identical layout suggests simultaneous death, perhaps by epidemic. Decorated sarcophagi of Ashayet and Kawit are in Cairo; Henhenet’s plain coffin is in New York.Kühn 2010, p. 23 f.D. Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975, p. 1015. === Tombs of Neferu and officials === Queen Neferu’s elaborate tomb (TT 319) was built at the north edge of the forecourt and later incorporated into Hatshepsut’s temple.Kühn 2010, p. 25. High officials were buried nearby in saff tombs aligned on the royal complex, notably those of vizier [[:en:Dagi|Dagi]] (TT 103), treasurer {{ill|Kheti|de|Cheti|ja|ヘティ|zh|赫蒂|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (TT 311) and steward [[:en:Henenu (high steward)|Henenu]] (TT 313).Kühn 2010, p. 27. == Reconstruction of the core == [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel-Naville-rawSketch.svg|thumb|left|Naville’s reconstruction with pyramid on the core]] Naville and Winlock envisaged a 7–8 m high core topped by a pyramid, citing the [[:en:Abbott Papyrus|Abbott Papyrus]] which calls the complex a pyramid. Arnold objects that no debris of such a structure exists and the core could not bear the thrust. He proposes a stylised primeval mound with flat terrace; [[:en:Rainer Stadelmann|Rainer Stadelmann]] adds a sand‑hump planted with trees. The tomb of [[:en:Nubkheperre Intef|Nubkheperre Intef]] discovered in 2000 renewed debate: it featured a small pyramid 11 m at base. {{ill|Gunnar Sperveslage|de|Gunnar Sperveslage|ja|グンナー・スペルフェスラーゲ|zh|古纳·斯佩尔费斯拉格|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} argues analogies favour a pyramid on Mentuhotep’s core, combining Theban saff tradition with Memphite pyramid symbolism.G. Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009), p. 68. == Cult == The complexity and poor preservation limit interpretation.Arnold 1974, p. 72. Given Mentuhotep’s devotion to [[:en:Montu|Month]], much of the temple honoured Month‑Ra.Ibid., p. 75. Amun‑Ra’s cult was served by priests from [[:en:Karnak|Karnak Temple]], making this a branch sanctuary.Ibid., p. 78 ff. The goddess [[:en:Hathor|Hathor]] features prominently, implying another Hathor shrine nearby.Ibid., p. 83 f. A collegiate body of lector and purification priests tended the royal cult, while Osirian elements appear especially in Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 72 ff., 80 f. Under Mentuhotep the [[:en:Beautiful Festival of the Valley|Valley Festival]] is first attested, when Amun‑Ra’s bark visited the king’s temple.S. Schott, *Das schöne Fest vom Wüstentale*, Mainz 1953, p. 94. == History == === Construction phases === Arnold identifies four phases: A pre‑unification east forecourt wall; Phase B with massive terracing, enclosure wall and Bab el‑Hosan as original tomb; Phases C & D after the king’s Sed‑festival added ambulatory, core, middle court, rear section and abandoned Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 62 ff. === Later use === After Mentuhotep the complex was converted to an Amun‑Ra shrine. [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]] honoured it with granite stela and statues. New Kingdom rulers again built at Deir el‑Bahari: [[:en:Amenhotep I|Amenhotep I]] erected a small shrine; [[:en:Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]]’s great temple overshadowed Mentuhotep’s; [[:en:Thutmose III|Thutmose III]] added his own mortuary temple. Demolition began under [[:en:Ramesses IV|Ramesses IV]] or [[:en:Ramesses VI|Ramesses VI]], probably to reuse stone downstream. Removing retaining walls triggered a landslide that buried the monument.Ibid., p. 67 ff. == Literature == (chronological order) === General === * Dieter Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep von Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. * Dieter Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975. * Dieter Arnold & Herbert E. Winlock, *The Temple of Mentuhotep at Deir el‑Bahari*, New York 1979. * Dieter Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens*, Munich 1992. * {{EAAE|Rosanna Pirelli|Deir el‑Bahri, Mentuhotep II complex|239–42}} * Dieter Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000. * Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010). === Monographs (with reviews) === * Édouard Naville, *The XIth Dynasty Temple at Deir El‑Bahari*, vol. 1, London 1907. * Édouard Naville, *ibid.*, vol. 2, London 1910. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, review of Arnold vol. 1 in *Die Welt des Orients* 8 (1975/76). * Eberhard Graefe, review in *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 38 (1981). === Specific studies === * Howard Carter, “Report on the Tomb of Mentuhotep Ist …,” *ASAE* 2 (1901). * Herbert E. Winlock, *Excavations at Deir el‑Bahari 1911–1931*, New York 1942. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, “Pyramiden im oberägyptischen Theben,” *Sokar* 5 (2002). * Gunnar Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009). == External links == {{Commonscat|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} * Mark Andrews: [http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/mentuhotept.htm The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II on the West Bank at Luxor] * Elke Noppes: [http://www.mentuhotep.de/ Mentuhotep Nebhepetre] (in German) * Thierry Benderitter: [http://www.osirisnet.net/monument/deb/mentuhotep/deb_mentuhotep.htm Deir el Bahari. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 2, Mainz 1974, p. 90. |BILD1 = MentuhotepII-Tempel.JPG |BILD1-BREITE = 290px |BILD1-BESCHREIBUNG = The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II at [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]] }} The '''Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II''' is a [[:en:Mortuary temple|mortuary temple]] built by [[:en:Mentuhotep II|Mentuhotep II]], an [[:en:Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] king ('''pharaoh''') of the [[:en:Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt|Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt]] during the [[:en:Middle Kingdom of Egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]]. The temple is located on the west bank of [[:en:Thebes, Egypt|Thebes, Egypt]] in the desert bay of [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]], close to the {{ill|Saff tomb|lt=saff tombs|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Mentuhotep’s ancestors. Architecturally and historically it marks the transition from the {{ill|pyramid temples|de|Pyramidentempel|ja|ピラミッド神殿|zh|金字塔神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:Old Kingdom of Egypt|Old Kingdom of Egypt]] to the {{ill|Million‑year house|de|Haus der Millionen|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|lt=million-year houses|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom of Egypt]].D. Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000, p. 159.D. Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens. Götterwohnungen – Baudenkmäler – Kultstätten*, Munich 1992, p. 140. It is the only substantially preserved monumental temple of the Middle Kingdom and served as a model for the [[:en:Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut|Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut]] built roughly 550 years later. Secondary use and a rock‑slide in the 20th Dynasty badly damaged the complex. == Research == [[File:Deir el Bahari-map.png|thumb|

Similar deposits under the core, cleared 1970, included linen inscribed with Mentuhotep’s and [[:en:Intef II|Intef II]]’s names.Ibid., Bd. 1, p. 52 ff. === The royal tomb === From the west court a 150 m sloping corridor leads to a granite burial chamber lined with rose granite and roofed corbel‑wise. Inside stood an alabaster shrine once sealed by double doors, which contained the wooden coffin and unpreserved funerary furniture of the king.Ibid., p. 44 ff.; Kühn 2010, p. 26. === Bab el‑Hosan === [[File:Bab el-Hosan.JPG|thumb|left|Entrance to Bab el‑Hosan (2010); background: Mentuhotep and Hatshepsut temples]] The Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), north of the causeway, was accidentally discovered when Carter’s horse fell through its roof in 1898. It is a secondary royal tomb: a 40 m shaft and 150 m sloping corridor leading west to a chamber where Carter found the black seated statue of the king and a deeper pit containing three wooden boats and pottery.Ibid., p. 51 ff. Arnold interprets it as an Osiris tomb providing the king magical resurrection.Ibid., p. 82. === Tomb of Tem === In the southwest corner of the hypostyle lies the tomb of the great wife Tem, aligned parallel to the king’s tomb and containing a colossal alabaster sarcophagus and a fragmentary offering slab.Ibid., p. 53 f. === Six tombs of queens and a princess === [[File:ShrineOfKemsit.jpg|thumb|Chapel of Kemsit (drawing by Margaret Naville)]] [[File:MentuhotepII-ShrineOfSadhe-Entrance.JPG|thumb|Entrance to the chapel of Sadeh (after Margaret Naville)]] Six richly decorated chapels with underground shaft‑tombs for the wives [[:en:Ashayet|Ashayet]], [[:en:Sadeh (queen)|Sadeh]], [[:en:Kawit (queen)|Kawit]], [[:en:Kemsit|Kemsit]], [[:en:Henhenet|Henhenet]] and princess {{ill|Mayet|de|Majit|ja|マイト|zh|马伊特|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were set into the west wall of the ambulatory. Their identical layout suggests simultaneous death, perhaps by epidemic. Decorated sarcophagi of Ashayet and Kawit are in Cairo; Henhenet’s plain coffin is in New York.Kühn 2010, p. 23 f.D. Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975, p. 1015. === Tombs of Neferu and officials === Queen Neferu’s elaborate tomb (TT 319) was built at the north edge of the forecourt and later incorporated into Hatshepsut’s temple.Kühn 2010, p. 25. High officials were buried nearby in saff tombs aligned on the royal complex, notably those of vizier [[:en:Dagi|Dagi]] (TT 103), treasurer {{ill|Kheti|de|Cheti|ja|ヘティ|zh|赫蒂|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (TT 311) and steward [[:en:Henenu (high steward)|Henenu]] (TT 313).Kühn 2010, p. 27. == Reconstruction of the core == [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel-Naville-rawSketch.svg|thumb|left|Naville’s reconstruction with pyramid on the core]] Naville and Winlock envisaged a 7–8 m high core topped by a pyramid, citing the [[:en:Abbott Papyrus|Abbott Papyrus]] which calls the complex a pyramid. Arnold objects that no debris of such a structure exists and the core could not bear the thrust. He proposes a stylised primeval mound with flat terrace; [[:en:Rainer Stadelmann|Rainer Stadelmann]] adds a sand‑hump planted with trees. The tomb of [[:en:Nubkheperre Intef|Nubkheperre Intef]] discovered in 2000 renewed debate: it featured a small pyramid 11 m at base. {{ill|Gunnar Sperveslage|de|Gunnar Sperveslage|ja|グンナー・スペルフェスラーゲ|zh|古纳·斯佩尔费斯拉格|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} argues analogies favour a pyramid on Mentuhotep’s core, combining Theban saff tradition with Memphite pyramid symbolism.G. Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009), p. 68. == Cult == The complexity and poor preservation limit interpretation.Arnold 1974, p. 72. Given Mentuhotep’s devotion to [[:en:Montu|Month]], much of the temple honoured Month‑Ra.Ibid., p. 75. Amun‑Ra’s cult was served by priests from [[:en:Karnak|Karnak Temple]], making this a branch sanctuary.Ibid., p. 78 ff. The goddess [[:en:Hathor|Hathor]] features prominently, implying another Hathor shrine nearby.Ibid., p. 83 f. A collegiate body of lector and purification priests tended the royal cult, while Osirian elements appear especially in Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 72 ff., 80 f. Under Mentuhotep the [[:en:Beautiful Festival of the Valley|Valley Festival]] is first attested, when Amun‑Ra’s bark visited the king’s temple.S. Schott, *Das schöne Fest vom Wüstentale*, Mainz 1953, p. 94. == History == === Construction phases === Arnold identifies four phases: A pre‑unification east forecourt wall; Phase B with massive terracing, enclosure wall and Bab el‑Hosan as original tomb; Phases C & D after the king’s Sed‑festival added ambulatory, core, middle court, rear section and abandoned Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 62 ff. === Later use === After Mentuhotep the complex was converted to an Amun‑Ra shrine. [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]] honoured it with granite stela and statues. New Kingdom rulers again built at Deir el‑Bahari: [[:en:Amenhotep I|Amenhotep I]] erected a small shrine; [[:en:Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]]’s great temple overshadowed Mentuhotep’s; [[:en:Thutmose III|Thutmose III]] added his own mortuary temple. Demolition began under [[:en:Ramesses IV|Ramesses IV]] or [[:en:Ramesses VI|Ramesses VI]], probably to reuse stone downstream. Removing retaining walls triggered a landslide that buried the monument.Ibid., p. 67 ff. == Literature == (chronological order) === General === * Dieter Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep von Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. * Dieter Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975. * Dieter Arnold & Herbert E. Winlock, *The Temple of Mentuhotep at Deir el‑Bahari*, New York 1979. * Dieter Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens*, Munich 1992. * {{EAAE|Rosanna Pirelli|Deir el‑Bahri, Mentuhotep II complex|239–42}} * Dieter Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000. * Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010). === Monographs (with reviews) === * Édouard Naville, *The XIth Dynasty Temple at Deir El‑Bahari*, vol. 1, London 1907. * Édouard Naville, *ibid.*, vol. 2, London 1910. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, review of Arnold vol. 1 in *Die Welt des Orients* 8 (1975/76). * Eberhard Graefe, review in *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 38 (1981). === Specific studies === * Howard Carter, “Report on the Tomb of Mentuhotep Ist …,” *ASAE* 2 (1901). * Herbert E. Winlock, *Excavations at Deir el‑Bahari 1911–1931*, New York 1942. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, “Pyramiden im oberägyptischen Theben,” *Sokar* 5 (2002). * Gunnar Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009). == External links == {{Commonscat|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} * Mark Andrews: [http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/mentuhotept.htm The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II on the West Bank at Luxor] * Elke Noppes: [http://www.mentuhotep.de/ Mentuhotep Nebhepetre] (in German) * Thierry Benderitter: [http://www.osirisnet.net/monument/deb/mentuhotep/deb_mentuhotep.htm Deir el Bahari. {{Infobox Hieroglyphen |NAME = G25-Aa1-Q1-Z1:Z1:Z1-V10A-N5-nb-P8-V11A |NAME-TRANSKRIPTION = Akh‑sut‑neb‑hepet‑Re
''3ḫ-swt-nb-ḥpt-Rˁ''
''Transfigured are the places of [[:en:Mentuhotep II|Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II]]'' |NAME2 = G25-st-t:Z2-M17-Y5:N35-G7-O24 |NAME2-TRANSKRIPTION= Akh‑sut‑Amun
''3ḫ-swt-Jmn''
''Transfigured are the places of [[:en:Amun|Amun]]''D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 2, Mainz 1974, p. 90. |BILD1 = MentuhotepII-Tempel.JPG |BILD1-BREITE = 290px |BILD1-BESCHREIBUNG = The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II at [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]] }} The '''Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II''' is a [[:en:Mortuary temple|mortuary temple]] built by [[:en:Mentuhotep II|Mentuhotep II]], an [[:en:Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] king ('''pharaoh''') of the [[:en:Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt|Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt]] during the [[:en:Middle Kingdom of Egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]]. The temple is located on the west bank of [[:en:Thebes, Egypt|Thebes, Egypt]] in the desert bay of [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]], close to the {{ill|Saff tomb|lt=saff tombs|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Mentuhotep’s ancestors. Architecturally and historically it marks the transition from the {{ill|pyramid temples|de|Pyramidentempel|ja|ピラミッド神殿|zh|金字塔神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:Old Kingdom of Egypt|Old Kingdom of Egypt]] to the {{ill|Million‑year house|de|Haus der Millionen|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|lt=million-year houses|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom of Egypt]].D. Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000, p. 159.D. Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens. Götterwohnungen – Baudenkmäler – Kultstätten*, Munich 1992, p. 140. It is the only substantially preserved monumental temple of the Middle Kingdom and served as a model for the [[:en:Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut|Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut]] built roughly 550 years later. Secondary use and a rock‑slide in the 20th Dynasty badly damaged the complex. == Research == [[File:Deir el Bahari-map.png|thumb|

'''II) Temple of Thutmose III'''
'''III) Temple of Hatshepsut''' Because the ruin was completely buried beneath rubble in the early 19th century, travellers did not realise that another temple lay hidden beside Hatshepsut’s. In 1858 workmen under [[:en:Auguste Mariette|Auguste Mariette]] discovered a cache of 72 mummy coffins belonging to priests of [[:en:Montu|Montu]] (22nd–26th Dynasties). In 1859 [[:en:Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|Lord Dufferin]] began excavations with Dr Lorange and Cyril C. Graham, clearing the southwest corner of the hypostyle, uncovering the plundered tomb of Queen [[:en:Tem (queen)|Tem]] and proceeding toward the sanctuary, where they found a seated statue of Amun‑Re and a granite altar of Mentuhotep. Further finds followed, including the tomb of [[:en:Neferu II|Neferu]] ([[:en:TT319|TT 319]]). In 1898 [[:en:Howard Carter|Howard Carter]] discovered the Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), clearing a mock burial and recovering the celebrated black seated statue of the king. [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel im Querschnitt.JPG|thumb|left|Cross‑section by Édouard Naville]] [[File:Mentuhotep-Tempel-Plan.JPG|thumb|Plan by Édouard Naville]] From 1903 to 1907 [[:en:Édouard Naville|Édouard Naville]] excavated the site for the Egypt Exploration Fund. Although Lord Dufferin had first revealed part of the plan, Naville was the first to expose and record the entire complex.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 1, Mainz 1974, p. 70. Between 1920 and 1931 [[:en:Herbert Eustis Winlock|Herbert E. Winlock]] led five seasons for the [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]], publishing only preliminary summaries.Ibid., p. 70 f. From 1967 to 1971 [[:en:Dieter Arnold|Dieter Arnold]] cleared and re‑studied the monument for the [[:en:German Archaeological Institute|German Archaeological Institute]], publishing his results in three volumes.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. == Architecture == === Causeway and forecourt === [[File:MentuhotepII-FuneraryStatue-CloseUp MetropolitanMuseum.png|thumb|left|upright|Head from a standing statue found in the forecourt (1921/22; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] [[File:Mentuhotep Deir el-Bahri.jpg|thumb|Aerial view of the temple]] [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel Sitzstatuen im Vorhof.JPG|thumb|Remains of two seated statues of Mentuhotep II in the forecourt]] Like its Old Kingdom predecessors, the complex possessed a sunken {{ill|Ancient Egyptian Valley Temple|lt=valley temple|de|Taltempel|ja|谷神殿|zh|峡谷神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and a 1.2 km long, 46 m wide processional {{ill|Causeway (Ancient Egypt|de|Aufweg|lt=causeway|it|Rampa processionale|cs|Vzestupná cesta}}, no longer roofed. The causeway ended in a vast forecourt enclosed by cliffs and planted with rows of trees and royal statues. Archaeology has identified pits for at least 57 [[:en:Tamarix|tamarisk]] and 6 [[:en:Ficus|sycomore fig]] and beds for flowers, allowing reconstruction of a rare [[:en:Gardens of ancient Egypt|temple garden]].H. Winlock in Arnold, *The Temple of Mentuhotep …*, New York 1979, p. 21 ff.Robichon–Varille in Arnold, *ibid.*, p. 21. A team of gardeners must have maintained irrigation from the Nile a kilometre away, creating greenery amid desert. At least twenty‑two seated sandstone statues of the king flanked the causeway, apparently crowned with the [[:en:Hedjet|White Crown of Upper Egypt]] on the south and the [[:en:Deshret|Red Crown of Lower Egypt]] on the north. One such statue found by Winlock in 1921/22 is now in New York.Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010), p. 21.
=== Eastern (front) section === West of the causeway lies the actual sanctuary, designed as a terrace temple in two parts. The front section was dedicated to [[:en:Montu|Month]]‑[[:en:Ra|Ra]], a fusion of the Theban war‑god and the sun‑god. The eastern façade presents colonnades on both sides of the ramp, each of two rows of square pillars evoking a {{ill|saff tomb|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 11 ff. A central ramp (Naville’s 1905 reconstruction) leads to the upper terrace, overlaying the original ramp whose lowest limestone revetment survives in two places.Ibid., p. 16 f. [[File:MentuhotepII-Reste des Ambulatoriums.JPG|thumb|Remains of the ambulatory and a corner of the core building]] On the terrace a 60 × 43 m, 5 m‑high podium supports the upper colonnade, a triple‑aisled {{ill|ambulatory|de|Ambulatorium|ja|周歩廊|zh|回廊|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the core building. The ambulatory comprised 140 octagonal pillars enclosed by a 5‑ell thick wall, creating a covered passage round the solid core. Entrances lay on east and west. Only bases or stumps of many pillars remain.Ibid., p. 21 f. The core, cleared in 1904/05, is a solid square block 22 m per side and 11 m high. Naville and Winlock reconstructed it as surmounted by a pyramid, but Arnold rejects this on structural grounds.Ibid., p. 27 ff.Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, p. 159.M. Höveler‑Müller, *Am Anfang war Ägypten*, Darmstadt 2013, p. 142. === Western (rear) section === [[File:MentuhotepII.jpg|thumb|Painted limestone block from the relief programme (Naville 1907; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] The rear portion, serving the cult of the deified king, was partly cut into the cliff and comprised an open court, a hypostyle with statue chapel, and later, a shrine to Amun‑Re, converting the complex into a true {{ill|million‑year house|de|Millionenjahrhaus|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 141. The middle court west of the ambulatory was flanked north and south by six columns and east by a double colonnade of eight columns. At its centre a deep [[:en:Dromos|dromos]] descends to the royal tomb. Finds include a limestone altar, a granite stele and six granite statues of [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]].Ibid., p. 33. West of the middle court lies the hypostyle hall (8 × 10 columns), separated by a wall and slightly higher.Ibid., p. 34 f. The sanctuary consists of a rock‑cut {{ill|speos|de|Speos|ja|スペオス|zh|石窟神殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} with a fore‑hall. All walls bore painted raised reliefs.D. Arnold, *ibid.*, Bd. 3, p. 15. Removing retaining walls triggered a landslide that buried the monument.Ibid., p. 67 ff. == Literature == (chronological order) === General === * Dieter Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep von Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. * Dieter Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975. * Dieter Arnold & Herbert E. Winlock, *The Temple of Mentuhotep at Deir el‑Bahari*, New York 1979. * Dieter Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens*, Munich 1992. * {{EAAE|Rosanna Pirelli|Deir el‑Bahri, Mentuhotep II complex|239–42}} * Dieter Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000. * Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010). === Monographs (with reviews) === * Édouard Naville, *The XIth Dynasty Temple at Deir El‑Bahari*, vol. 1, London 1907. * Édouard Naville, *ibid.*, vol. 2, London 1910. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, review of Arnold vol. 1 in *Die Welt des Orients* 8 (1975/76). * Eberhard Graefe, review in *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 38 (1981). === Specific studies === * Howard Carter, “Report on the Tomb of Mentuhotep Ist …,” *ASAE* 2 (1901). * Herbert E. Winlock, *Excavations at Deir el‑Bahari 1911–1931*, New York 1942. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, “Pyramiden im oberägyptischen Theben,” *Sokar* 5 (2002). * Gunnar Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009). == External links == {{Commonscat|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} * Mark Andrews: [http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/mentuhotept.htm The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II on the West Bank at Luxor] * Elke Noppes: [http://www.mentuhotep.de/ Mentuhotep Nebhepetre] (in German) * Thierry Benderitter: [http://www.osirisnet.net/monument/deb/mentuhotep/deb_mentuhotep.htm Deir el Bahari. [[ar:المعبد الجنائزي لمنتوحوتب الثاني]][[arz:المعبد الجنائزى لمنتوحوتب التانى]][[commons:Category:Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II]][[de:Totentempel des Mentuhotep II.]][[es:Templo funerario de Mentuhotep II]][[fr:Temple funéraire de Montouhotep II]][[sq:Tempulli mortor i Montuhotepit të II]][[ur:معبد جنائزی آمون حوتپ دوم]] {{Infobox Hieroglyphen |NAME = G25-Aa1-Q1-Z1:Z1:Z1-V10A-N5-nb-P8-V11A |NAME-TRANSKRIPTION = Akh‑sut‑neb‑hepet‑Re
''3ḫ-swt-nb-ḥpt-Rˁ''
''Transfigured are the places of [[:en:Mentuhotep II|Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II]]'' |NAME2 = G25-st-t:Z2-M17-Y5:N35-G7-O24 |NAME2-TRANSKRIPTION= Akh‑sut‑Amun
''3ḫ-swt-Jmn''
''Transfigured are the places of [[:en:Amun|Amun]]''D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 2, Mainz 1974, p. 90. |BILD1 = MentuhotepII-Tempel.JPG |BILD1-BREITE = 290px |BILD1-BESCHREIBUNG = The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II at [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]] }} The '''Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II''' is a [[:en:Mortuary temple|mortuary temple]] built by [[:en:Mentuhotep II|Mentuhotep II]], an [[:en:Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] king ('''pharaoh''') of the [[:en:Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt|Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt]] during the [[:en:Middle Kingdom of Egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]]. The temple is located on the west bank of [[:en:Thebes, Egypt|Thebes, Egypt]] in the desert bay of [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]], close to the {{ill|Saff tomb|lt=saff tombs|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Mentuhotep’s ancestors. Architecturally and historically it marks the transition from the {{ill|pyramid temples|de|Pyramidentempel|ja|ピラミッド神殿|zh|金字塔神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:Old Kingdom of Egypt|Old Kingdom of Egypt]] to the {{ill|Million‑year house|de|Haus der Millionen|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|lt=million-year houses|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom of Egypt]].D. Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000, p. 159.D. Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens. Götterwohnungen – Baudenkmäler – Kultstätten*, Munich 1992, p. 140. It is the only substantially preserved monumental temple of the Middle Kingdom and served as a model for the [[:en:Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut|Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut]] built roughly 550 years later. Secondary use and a rock‑slide in the 20th Dynasty badly damaged the complex. == Research == [[File:Deir el Bahari-map.png|thumb|
Map of Deir el‑Bahari
]] '''I) Temple of Mentuhotep II'''

2) Lower colonnades (either side of the processional ramp)

'''II) Temple of Thutmose III'''
'''III) Temple of Hatshepsut''' Because the ruin was completely buried beneath rubble in the early 19th century, travellers did not realise that another temple lay hidden beside Hatshepsut’s. In 1858 workmen under [[:en:Auguste Mariette|Auguste Mariette]] discovered a cache of 72 mummy coffins belonging to priests of [[:en:Montu|Montu]] (22nd–26th Dynasties). In 1859 [[:en:Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|Lord Dufferin]] began excavations with Dr Lorange and Cyril C. Graham, clearing the southwest corner of the hypostyle, uncovering the plundered tomb of Queen [[:en:Tem (queen)|Tem]] and proceeding toward the sanctuary, where they found a seated statue of Amun‑Re and a granite altar of Mentuhotep. Further finds followed, including the tomb of [[:en:Neferu II|Neferu]] ([[:en:TT319|TT 319]]). In 1898 [[:en:Howard Carter|Howard Carter]] discovered the Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), clearing a mock burial and recovering the celebrated black seated statue of the king. [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel im Querschnitt.JPG|thumb|left|Cross‑section by Édouard Naville]] [[File:Mentuhotep-Tempel-Plan.JPG|thumb|Plan by Édouard Naville]] From 1903 to 1907 [[:en:Édouard Naville|Édouard Naville]] excavated the site for the Egypt Exploration Fund. Although Lord Dufferin had first revealed part of the plan, Naville was the first to expose and record the entire complex.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 1, Mainz 1974, p. 70. Between 1920 and 1931 [[:en:Herbert Eustis Winlock|Herbert E. Winlock]] led five seasons for the [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]], publishing only preliminary summaries.Ibid., p. 70 f. From 1967 to 1971 [[:en:Dieter Arnold|Dieter Arnold]] cleared and re‑studied the monument for the [[:en:German Archaeological Institute|German Archaeological Institute]], publishing his results in three volumes.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. == Architecture == === Causeway and forecourt === [[File:MentuhotepII-FuneraryStatue-CloseUp MetropolitanMuseum.png|thumb|left|upright|Head from a standing statue found in the forecourt (1921/22; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] [[File:Mentuhotep Deir el-Bahri.jpg|thumb|Aerial view of the temple]] [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel Sitzstatuen im Vorhof.JPG|thumb|Remains of two seated statues of Mentuhotep II in the forecourt]] Like its Old Kingdom predecessors, the complex possessed a sunken {{ill|Ancient Egyptian Valley Temple|lt=valley temple|de|Taltempel|ja|谷神殿|zh|峡谷神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and a 1.2 km long, 46 m wide processional {{ill|Causeway (Ancient Egypt|de|Aufweg|lt=causeway|it|Rampa processionale|cs|Vzestupná cesta}}, no longer roofed. The causeway ended in a vast forecourt enclosed by cliffs and planted with rows of trees and royal statues. Archaeology has identified pits for at least 57 [[:en:Tamarix|tamarisk]] and 6 [[:en:Ficus|sycomore fig]] and beds for flowers, allowing reconstruction of a rare [[:en:Gardens of ancient Egypt|temple garden]].H. Winlock in Arnold, *The Temple of Mentuhotep …*, New York 1979, p. 21 ff.Robichon–Varille in Arnold, *ibid.*, p. 21. A team of gardeners must have maintained irrigation from the Nile a kilometre away, creating greenery amid desert. At least twenty‑two seated sandstone statues of the king flanked the causeway, apparently crowned with the [[:en:Hedjet|White Crown of Upper Egypt]] on the south and the [[:en:Deshret|Red Crown of Lower Egypt]] on the north. One such statue found by Winlock in 1921/22 is now in New York.Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010), p. 21.
=== Eastern (front) section === West of the causeway lies the actual sanctuary, designed as a terrace temple in two parts. The front section was dedicated to [[:en:Montu|Month]]‑[[:en:Ra|Ra]], a fusion of the Theban war‑god and the sun‑god. The eastern façade presents colonnades on both sides of the ramp, each of two rows of square pillars evoking a {{ill|saff tomb|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 11 ff. A central ramp (Naville’s 1905 reconstruction) leads to the upper terrace, overlaying the original ramp whose lowest limestone revetment survives in two places.Ibid., p. 16 f. [[File:MentuhotepII-Reste des Ambulatoriums.JPG|thumb|Remains of the ambulatory and a corner of the core building]] On the terrace a 60 × 43 m, 5 m‑high podium supports the upper colonnade, a triple‑aisled {{ill|ambulatory|de|Ambulatorium|ja|周歩廊|zh|回廊|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the core building. The ambulatory comprised 140 octagonal pillars enclosed by a 5‑ell thick wall, creating a covered passage round the solid core. Entrances lay on east and west. Only bases or stumps of many pillars remain.Ibid., p. 21 f. The core, cleared in 1904/05, is a solid square block 22 m per side and 11 m high. Naville and Winlock reconstructed it as surmounted by a pyramid, but Arnold rejects this on structural grounds.Ibid., p. 27 ff.Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, p. 159.M. Höveler‑Müller, *Am Anfang war Ägypten*, Darmstadt 2013, p. 142. === Western (rear) section === [[File:MentuhotepII.jpg|thumb|Painted limestone block from the relief programme (Naville 1907; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] The rear portion, serving the cult of the deified king, was partly cut into the cliff and comprised an open court, a hypostyle with statue chapel, and later, a shrine to Amun‑Re, converting the complex into a true {{ill|million‑year house|de|Millionenjahrhaus|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 141. The middle court west of the ambulatory was flanked north and south by six columns and east by a double colonnade of eight columns. At its centre a deep [[:en:Dromos|dromos]] descends to the royal tomb. Finds include a limestone altar, a granite stele and six granite statues of [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]].Ibid., p. 33. West of the middle court lies the hypostyle hall (8 × 10 columns), separated by a wall and slightly higher.Ibid., p. 34 f. The sanctuary consists of a rock‑cut {{ill|speos|de|Speos|ja|スペオス|zh|石窟神殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} with a fore‑hall. All walls bore painted raised reliefs.D. Arnold, *ibid.*, Bd. 3, p. 15. Fragments show the king receiving cult as a god among gods.Ibid., p. 16. The statue room yielded an over‑life‑size standing statue of the king and a seated image of Amun‑Re, perhaps another royal theophany.Ibid., p. 33 f. === Foundation deposits === Under the terrace corners Winlock discovered intact foundation pits containing cattle skulls, food offerings, bricks and inscribed objects.Ibid., Bd. 3, p. 49 ff. Similar deposits under the core, cleared 1970, included linen inscribed with Mentuhotep’s and [[:en:Intef II|Intef II]]’s names.Ibid., Bd. 1, p. 52 ff. === The royal tomb === From the west court a 150 m sloping corridor leads to a granite burial chamber lined with rose granite and roofed corbel‑wise. Inside stood an alabaster shrine once sealed by double doors, which contained the wooden coffin and unpreserved funerary furniture of the king.Ibid., p. 44 ff.; Kühn 2010, p. 26. === Bab el‑Hosan === [[File:Bab el-Hosan.JPG|thumb|left|Entrance to Bab el‑Hosan (2010); background: Mentuhotep and Hatshepsut temples]] The Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), north of the causeway, was accidentally discovered when Carter’s horse fell through its roof in 1898. It is a secondary royal tomb: a 40 m shaft and 150 m sloping corridor leading west to a chamber where Carter found the black seated statue of the king and a deeper pit containing three wooden boats and pottery.Ibid., p. 51 ff. Arnold interprets it as an Osiris tomb providing the king magical resurrection.Ibid., p. 82. === Tomb of Tem === In the southwest corner of the hypostyle lies the tomb of the great wife Tem, aligned parallel to the king’s tomb and containing a colossal alabaster sarcophagus and a fragmentary offering slab.Ibid., p. 53 f. === Six tombs of queens and a princess === [[File:ShrineOfKemsit.jpg|thumb|Chapel of Kemsit (drawing by Margaret Naville)]] [[File:MentuhotepII-ShrineOfSadhe-Entrance.JPG|thumb|Entrance to the chapel of Sadeh (after Margaret Naville)]] Six richly decorated chapels with underground shaft‑tombs for the wives [[:en:Ashayet|Ashayet]], [[:en:Sadeh (queen)|Sadeh]], [[:en:Kawit (queen)|Kawit]], [[:en:Kemsit|Kemsit]], [[:en:Henhenet|Henhenet]] and princess {{ill|Mayet|de|Majit|ja|マイト|zh|马伊特|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were set into the west wall of the ambulatory. Their identical layout suggests simultaneous death, perhaps by epidemic. Decorated sarcophagi of Ashayet and Kawit are in Cairo; Henhenet’s plain coffin is in New York.Kühn 2010, p. 23 f.D. Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975, p. 1015. === Tombs of Neferu and officials === Queen Neferu’s elaborate tomb (TT 319) was built at the north edge of the forecourt and later incorporated into Hatshepsut’s temple.Kühn 2010, p. 25. High officials were buried nearby in saff tombs aligned on the royal complex, notably those of vizier [[:en:Dagi|Dagi]] (TT 103), treasurer {{ill|Kheti|de|Cheti|ja|ヘティ|zh|赫蒂|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (TT 311) and steward [[:en:Henenu (high steward)|Henenu]] (TT 313).Kühn 2010, p. 27. == Reconstruction of the core == [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel-Naville-rawSketch.svg|thumb|left|Naville’s reconstruction with pyramid on the core]] Naville and Winlock envisaged a 7–8 m high core topped by a pyramid, citing the [[:en:Abbott Papyrus|Abbott Papyrus]] which calls the complex a pyramid. Arnold objects that no debris of such a structure exists and the core could not bear the thrust. He proposes a stylised primeval mound with flat terrace; [[:en:Rainer Stadelmann|Rainer Stadelmann]] adds a sand‑hump planted with trees. The tomb of [[:en:Nubkheperre Intef|Nubkheperre Intef]] discovered in 2000 renewed debate: it featured a small pyramid 11 m at base. {{ill|Gunnar Sperveslage|de|Gunnar Sperveslage|ja|グンナー・スペルフェスラーゲ|zh|古纳·斯佩尔费斯拉格|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} argues analogies favour a pyramid on Mentuhotep’s core, combining Theban saff tradition with Memphite pyramid symbolism.G. Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009), p. 68. == Cult == The complexity and poor preservation limit interpretation.Arnold 1974, p. 72. Given Mentuhotep’s devotion to [[:en:Montu|Month]], much of the temple honoured Month‑Ra.Ibid., p. 75. Amun‑Ra’s cult was served by priests from [[:en:Karnak|Karnak Temple]], making this a branch sanctuary.Ibid., p. 78 ff. The goddess [[:en:Hathor|Hathor]] features prominently, implying another Hathor shrine nearby.Ibid., p. 83 f. A collegiate body of lector and purification priests tended the royal cult, while Osirian elements appear especially in Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 72 ff., 80 f. Under Mentuhotep the [[:en:Beautiful Festival of the Valley|Valley Festival]] is first attested, when Amun‑Ra’s bark visited the king’s temple.S. Schott, *Das schöne Fest vom Wüstentale*, Mainz 1953, p. 94. == History == === Construction phases === Arnold identifies four phases: A pre‑unification east forecourt wall; Phase B with massive terracing, enclosure wall and Bab el‑Hosan as original tomb; Phases C & D after the king’s Sed‑festival added ambulatory, core, middle court, rear section and abandoned Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 62 ff. === Later use === After Mentuhotep the complex was converted to an Amun‑Ra shrine. [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]] honoured it with granite stela and statues. New Kingdom rulers again built at Deir el‑Bahari: [[:en:Amenhotep I|Amenhotep I]] erected a small shrine; [[:en:Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]]’s great temple overshadowed Mentuhotep’s; [[:en:Thutmose III|Thutmose III]] added his own mortuary temple. Demolition began under [[:en:Ramesses IV|Ramesses IV]] or [[:en:Ramesses VI|Ramesses VI]], probably to reuse stone downstream. Removing retaining walls triggered a landslide that buried the monument.Ibid., p. 67 ff. == Literature == (chronological order) === General === * Dieter Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep von Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. * Dieter Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975. * Dieter Arnold & Herbert E. Winlock, *The Temple of Mentuhotep at Deir el‑Bahari*, New York 1979. * Dieter Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens*, Munich 1992. * {{EAAE|Rosanna Pirelli|Deir el‑Bahri, Mentuhotep II complex|239–42}} * Dieter Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000. * Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010). === Monographs (with reviews) === * Édouard Naville, *The XIth Dynasty Temple at Deir El‑Bahari*, vol. 1, London 1907. * Édouard Naville, *ibid.*, vol. 2, London 1910. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, review of Arnold vol. 1 in *Die Welt des Orients* 8 (1975/76). * Eberhard Graefe, review in *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 38 (1981). === Specific studies === * Howard Carter, “Report on the Tomb of Mentuhotep Ist …,” *ASAE* 2 (1901). * Herbert E. Winlock, *Excavations at Deir el‑Bahari 1911–1931*, New York 1942. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, “Pyramiden im oberägyptischen Theben,” *Sokar* 5 (2002). * Gunnar Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009). == External links == {{Commonscat|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} * Mark Andrews: [http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/mentuhotept.htm The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II on the West Bank at Luxor] * Elke Noppes: [http://www.mentuhotep.de/ Mentuhotep Nebhepetre] (in German) * Thierry Benderitter: [http://www.osirisnet.net/monument/deb/mentuhotep/deb_mentuhotep.htm Deir el Bahari. The temple is located on the west bank of [[:en:Thebes, Egypt|Thebes, Egypt]] in the desert bay of [[:en:Deir el-Bahari|Deir el‑Bahari]], close to the {{ill|Saff tomb|lt=saff tombs|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Mentuhotep’s ancestors. Architecturally and historically it marks the transition from the {{ill|pyramid temples|de|Pyramidentempel|ja|ピラミッド神殿|zh|金字塔神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:Old Kingdom of Egypt|Old Kingdom of Egypt]] to the {{ill|Million‑year house|de|Haus der Millionen|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|lt=million-year houses|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of the [[:en:New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom of Egypt]].D. Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000, p. 159.D. Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens. Götterwohnungen – Baudenkmäler – Kultstätten*, Munich 1992, p. 140. It is the only substantially preserved monumental temple of the Middle Kingdom and served as a model for the [[:en:Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut|Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut]] built roughly 550 years later. Secondary use and a rock‑slide in the 20th Dynasty badly damaged the complex. == Research == [[File:Deir el Bahari-map.png|thumb|
Map of Deir el‑Bahari
]] '''I) Temple of Mentuhotep II'''
1) Bab el‑Hosan
2) Lower colonnades (either side of the processional ramp)
3) Upper colonnade
Between 3) and 4) Ambulatory
4) Core building
Between 4) and 5) Middle court with dromos leading to the royal tomb

6) Sanctuary
'''II) Temple of Thutmose III'''
'''III) Temple of Hatshepsut''' Because the ruin was completely buried beneath rubble in the early 19th century, travellers did not realise that another temple lay hidden beside Hatshepsut’s. In 1858 workmen under [[:en:Auguste Mariette|Auguste Mariette]] discovered a cache of 72 mummy coffins belonging to priests of [[:en:Montu|Montu]] (22nd–26th Dynasties). In 1859 [[:en:Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|Lord Dufferin]] began excavations with Dr Lorange and Cyril C. Graham, clearing the southwest corner of the hypostyle, uncovering the plundered tomb of Queen [[:en:Tem (queen)|Tem]] and proceeding toward the sanctuary, where they found a seated statue of Amun‑Re and a granite altar of Mentuhotep. Further finds followed, including the tomb of [[:en:Neferu II|Neferu]] ([[:en:TT319|TT 319]]). In 1898 [[:en:Howard Carter|Howard Carter]] discovered the Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), clearing a mock burial and recovering the celebrated black seated statue of the king. [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel im Querschnitt.JPG|thumb|left|Cross‑section by Édouard Naville]] [[File:Mentuhotep-Tempel-Plan.JPG|thumb|Plan by Édouard Naville]] From 1903 to 1907 [[:en:Édouard Naville|Édouard Naville]] excavated the site for the Egypt Exploration Fund. Although Lord Dufferin had first revealed part of the plan, Naville was the first to expose and record the entire complex.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, Bd. 1, Mainz 1974, p. 70. Between 1920 and 1931 [[:en:Herbert Eustis Winlock|Herbert E. Winlock]] led five seasons for the [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]], publishing only preliminary summaries.Ibid., p. 70 f. From 1967 to 1971 [[:en:Dieter Arnold|Dieter Arnold]] cleared and re‑studied the monument for the [[:en:German Archaeological Institute|German Archaeological Institute]], publishing his results in three volumes.D. Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep in Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. == Architecture == === Causeway and forecourt === [[File:MentuhotepII-FuneraryStatue-CloseUp MetropolitanMuseum.png|thumb|left|upright|Head from a standing statue found in the forecourt (1921/22; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] [[File:Mentuhotep Deir el-Bahri.jpg|thumb|Aerial view of the temple]] [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel Sitzstatuen im Vorhof.JPG|thumb|Remains of two seated statues of Mentuhotep II in the forecourt]] Like its Old Kingdom predecessors, the complex possessed a sunken {{ill|Ancient Egyptian Valley Temple|lt=valley temple|de|Taltempel|ja|谷神殿|zh|峡谷神庙|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and a 1.2 km long, 46 m wide processional {{ill|Causeway (Ancient Egypt|de|Aufweg|lt=causeway|it|Rampa processionale|cs|Vzestupná cesta}}, no longer roofed. The causeway ended in a vast forecourt enclosed by cliffs and planted with rows of trees and royal statues. Archaeology has identified pits for at least 57 [[:en:Tamarix|tamarisk]] and 6 [[:en:Ficus|sycomore fig]] and beds for flowers, allowing reconstruction of a rare [[:en:Gardens of ancient Egypt|temple garden]].H. Winlock in Arnold, *The Temple of Mentuhotep …*, New York 1979, p. 21 ff.Robichon–Varille in Arnold, *ibid.*, p. 21. A team of gardeners must have maintained irrigation from the Nile a kilometre away, creating greenery amid desert. At least twenty‑two seated sandstone statues of the king flanked the causeway, apparently crowned with the [[:en:Hedjet|White Crown of Upper Egypt]] on the south and the [[:en:Deshret|Red Crown of Lower Egypt]] on the north. One such statue found by Winlock in 1921/22 is now in New York.Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010), p. 21.
=== Eastern (front) section === West of the causeway lies the actual sanctuary, designed as a terrace temple in two parts. The front section was dedicated to [[:en:Montu|Month]]‑[[:en:Ra|Ra]], a fusion of the Theban war‑god and the sun‑god. The eastern façade presents colonnades on both sides of the ramp, each of two rows of square pillars evoking a {{ill|saff tomb|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 11 ff. A central ramp (Naville’s 1905 reconstruction) leads to the upper terrace, overlaying the original ramp whose lowest limestone revetment survives in two places.Ibid., p. 16 f. [[File:MentuhotepII-Reste des Ambulatoriums.JPG|thumb|Remains of the ambulatory and a corner of the core building]] On the terrace a 60 × 43 m, 5 m‑high podium supports the upper colonnade, a triple‑aisled {{ill|ambulatory|de|Ambulatorium|ja|周歩廊|zh|回廊|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the core building. The ambulatory comprised 140 octagonal pillars enclosed by a 5‑ell thick wall, creating a covered passage round the solid core. Entrances lay on east and west. Only bases or stumps of many pillars remain.Ibid., p. 21 f. The core, cleared in 1904/05, is a solid square block 22 m per side and 11 m high. Naville and Winlock reconstructed it as surmounted by a pyramid, but Arnold rejects this on structural grounds.Ibid., p. 27 ff.Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, p. 159.M. Höveler‑Müller, *Am Anfang war Ägypten*, Darmstadt 2013, p. 142. === Western (rear) section === [[File:MentuhotepII.jpg|thumb|Painted limestone block from the relief programme (Naville 1907; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] The rear portion, serving the cult of the deified king, was partly cut into the cliff and comprised an open court, a hypostyle with statue chapel, and later, a shrine to Amun‑Re, converting the complex into a true {{ill|million‑year house|de|Millionenjahrhaus|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 141. The middle court west of the ambulatory was flanked north and south by six columns and east by a double colonnade of eight columns. At its centre a deep [[:en:Dromos|dromos]] descends to the royal tomb. Finds include a limestone altar, a granite stele and six granite statues of [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]].Ibid., p. 33. West of the middle court lies the hypostyle hall (8 × 10 columns), separated by a wall and slightly higher.Ibid., p. 34 f. The sanctuary consists of a rock‑cut {{ill|speos|de|Speos|ja|スペオス|zh|石窟神殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} with a fore‑hall. All walls bore painted raised reliefs.D. Arnold, *ibid.*, Bd. 3, p. 15. Fragments show the king receiving cult as a god among gods.Ibid., p. 16. The statue room yielded an over‑life‑size standing statue of the king and a seated image of Amun‑Re, perhaps another royal theophany.Ibid., p. 33 f. === Foundation deposits === Under the terrace corners Winlock discovered intact foundation pits containing cattle skulls, food offerings, bricks and inscribed objects.Ibid., Bd. 3, p. 49 ff. Similar deposits under the core, cleared 1970, included linen inscribed with Mentuhotep’s and [[:en:Intef II|Intef II]]’s names.Ibid., Bd. 1, p. 52 ff. === The royal tomb === From the west court a 150 m sloping corridor leads to a granite burial chamber lined with rose granite and roofed corbel‑wise. Inside stood an alabaster shrine once sealed by double doors, which contained the wooden coffin and unpreserved funerary furniture of the king.Ibid., p. 44 ff.; Kühn 2010, p. 26. === Bab el‑Hosan === [[File:Bab el-Hosan.JPG|thumb|left|Entrance to Bab el‑Hosan (2010); background: Mentuhotep and Hatshepsut temples]] The Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), north of the causeway, was accidentally discovered when Carter’s horse fell through its roof in 1898. It is a secondary royal tomb: a 40 m shaft and 150 m sloping corridor leading west to a chamber where Carter found the black seated statue of the king and a deeper pit containing three wooden boats and pottery.Ibid., p. 51 ff. Arnold interprets it as an Osiris tomb providing the king magical resurrection.Ibid., p. 82. === Tomb of Tem === In the southwest corner of the hypostyle lies the tomb of the great wife Tem, aligned parallel to the king’s tomb and containing a colossal alabaster sarcophagus and a fragmentary offering slab.Ibid., p. 53 f. === Six tombs of queens and a princess === [[File:ShrineOfKemsit.jpg|thumb|Chapel of Kemsit (drawing by Margaret Naville)]] [[File:MentuhotepII-ShrineOfSadhe-Entrance.JPG|thumb|Entrance to the chapel of Sadeh (after Margaret Naville)]] Six richly decorated chapels with underground shaft‑tombs for the wives [[:en:Ashayet|Ashayet]], [[:en:Sadeh (queen)|Sadeh]], [[:en:Kawit (queen)|Kawit]], [[:en:Kemsit|Kemsit]], [[:en:Henhenet|Henhenet]] and princess {{ill|Mayet|de|Majit|ja|マイト|zh|马伊特|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were set into the west wall of the ambulatory. Their identical layout suggests simultaneous death, perhaps by epidemic. Decorated sarcophagi of Ashayet and Kawit are in Cairo; Henhenet’s plain coffin is in New York.Kühn 2010, p. 23 f.D. Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975, p. 1015. === Tombs of Neferu and officials === Queen Neferu’s elaborate tomb (TT 319) was built at the north edge of the forecourt and later incorporated into Hatshepsut’s temple.Kühn 2010, p. 25. High officials were buried nearby in saff tombs aligned on the royal complex, notably those of vizier [[:en:Dagi|Dagi]] (TT 103), treasurer {{ill|Kheti|de|Cheti|ja|ヘティ|zh|赫蒂|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (TT 311) and steward [[:en:Henenu (high steward)|Henenu]] (TT 313).Kühn 2010, p. 27. == Reconstruction of the core == [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel-Naville-rawSketch.svg|thumb|left|Naville’s reconstruction with pyramid on the core]] Naville and Winlock envisaged a 7–8 m high core topped by a pyramid, citing the [[:en:Abbott Papyrus|Abbott Papyrus]] which calls the complex a pyramid. Arnold objects that no debris of such a structure exists and the core could not bear the thrust. He proposes a stylised primeval mound with flat terrace; [[:en:Rainer Stadelmann|Rainer Stadelmann]] adds a sand‑hump planted with trees. The tomb of [[:en:Nubkheperre Intef|Nubkheperre Intef]] discovered in 2000 renewed debate: it featured a small pyramid 11 m at base. {{ill|Gunnar Sperveslage|de|Gunnar Sperveslage|ja|グンナー・スペルフェスラーゲ|zh|古纳·斯佩尔费斯拉格|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} argues analogies favour a pyramid on Mentuhotep’s core, combining Theban saff tradition with Memphite pyramid symbolism.G. Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009), p. 68. == Cult == The complexity and poor preservation limit interpretation.Arnold 1974, p. 72. Given Mentuhotep’s devotion to [[:en:Montu|Month]], much of the temple honoured Month‑Ra.Ibid., p. 75. Amun‑Ra’s cult was served by priests from [[:en:Karnak|Karnak Temple]], making this a branch sanctuary.Ibid., p. 78 ff. The goddess [[:en:Hathor|Hathor]] features prominently, implying another Hathor shrine nearby.Ibid., p. 83 f. A collegiate body of lector and purification priests tended the royal cult, while Osirian elements appear especially in Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 72 ff., 80 f. Under Mentuhotep the [[:en:Beautiful Festival of the Valley|Valley Festival]] is first attested, when Amun‑Ra’s bark visited the king’s temple.S. Schott, *Das schöne Fest vom Wüstentale*, Mainz 1953, p. 94. == History == === Construction phases === Arnold identifies four phases: A pre‑unification east forecourt wall; Phase B with massive terracing, enclosure wall and Bab el‑Hosan as original tomb; Phases C & D after the king’s Sed‑festival added ambulatory, core, middle court, rear section and abandoned Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 62 ff. === Later use === After Mentuhotep the complex was converted to an Amun‑Ra shrine. [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]] honoured it with granite stela and statues. New Kingdom rulers again built at Deir el‑Bahari: [[:en:Amenhotep I|Amenhotep I]] erected a small shrine; [[:en:Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]]’s great temple overshadowed Mentuhotep’s; [[:en:Thutmose III|Thutmose III]] added his own mortuary temple. Demolition began under [[:en:Ramesses IV|Ramesses IV]] or [[:en:Ramesses VI|Ramesses VI]], probably to reuse stone downstream. Removing retaining walls triggered a landslide that buried the monument.Ibid., p. 67 ff. == Literature == (chronological order) === General === * Dieter Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep von Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. * Dieter Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975. * Dieter Arnold & Herbert E. Winlock, *The Temple of Mentuhotep at Deir el‑Bahari*, New York 1979. * Dieter Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens*, Munich 1992. * {{EAAE|Rosanna Pirelli|Deir el‑Bahri, Mentuhotep II complex|239–42}} * Dieter Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000. * Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010). === Monographs (with reviews) === * Édouard Naville, *The XIth Dynasty Temple at Deir El‑Bahari*, vol. 1, London 1907. * Édouard Naville, *ibid.*, vol. 2, London 1910. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, review of Arnold vol. 1 in *Die Welt des Orients* 8 (1975/76). * Eberhard Graefe, review in *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 38 (1981). === Specific studies === * Howard Carter, “Report on the Tomb of Mentuhotep Ist …,” *ASAE* 2 (1901). * Herbert E. Winlock, *Excavations at Deir el‑Bahari 1911–1931*, New York 1942. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, “Pyramiden im oberägyptischen Theben,” *Sokar* 5 (2002). * Gunnar Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009). == External links == {{Commonscat|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} * Mark Andrews: [http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/mentuhotept.htm The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II on the West Bank at Luxor] * Elke Noppes: [http://www.mentuhotep.de/ Mentuhotep Nebhepetre] (in German) * Thierry Benderitter: [http://www.osirisnet.net/monument/deb/mentuhotep/deb_mentuhotep.htm Deir el Bahari. Le Temple de Mentouhotep] (in French) * [http://wysinger.homestead.com/mentuhotep.html Mentuhotep II & Wives] (homestead.com) * Theban Mapping Project: [http://www.tmpbibliography.com/resources/bibliography_4mt_mortuary_temples_a_dayr_al_bahri.html Bibliography for Dayr el‑Bahri] * Archaeowiki: {{Webarchiv|url=http://www.archaeowiki.org/Carter%27s_Description_of_the_Discovery_of_the_Bab_el-Hosan|wayback=20100829175145|text=Carter’s Description of the Discovery of the Bab el‑Hosan}} == Notes == {{Coordinate|NS=25/44/14.5/N|EW=32/36/22/E|type=landmark|region=EG-KN}} [[Category:completion tier 1]] [[Category:Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt]] [[Category:21st-century BC architecture]] [[Category:Forschungsprojekt des Deutschen Archäologischen Instituts]] [[Category:Tempel in Theben-West]] [[Category:Temples by person]] [[arz:المعبد الجنائزى لمنتوحوتب التانى]] {{Commons category|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} [[en:Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II]] {{wikidata link|Q14551916}}[[de:Totentempel des Mentuhotep II.]]

At least twenty‑two seated sandstone statues of the king flanked the causeway, apparently crowned with the [[:en:Hedjet|White Crown of Upper Egypt]] on the south and the [[:en:Deshret|Red Crown of Lower Egypt]] on the north. One such statue found by Winlock in 1921/22 is now in New York.Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010), p. 21.
=== Eastern (front) section === West of the causeway lies the actual sanctuary, designed as a terrace temple in two parts. The front section was dedicated to [[:en:Montu|Month]]‑[[:en:Ra|Ra]], a fusion of the Theban war‑god and the sun‑god. The eastern façade presents colonnades on both sides of the ramp, each of two rows of square pillars evoking a {{ill|saff tomb|de|Saff-Grab|ja|サフ墓|zh|萨夫墓|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 11 ff. A central ramp (Naville’s 1905 reconstruction) leads to the upper terrace, overlaying the original ramp whose lowest limestone revetment survives in two places.Ibid., p. 16 f. [[File:MentuhotepII-Reste des Ambulatoriums.JPG|thumb|Remains of the ambulatory and a corner of the core building]] On the terrace a 60 × 43 m, 5 m‑high podium supports the upper colonnade, a triple‑aisled {{ill|ambulatory|de|Ambulatorium|ja|周歩廊|zh|回廊|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the core building. The ambulatory comprised 140 octagonal pillars enclosed by a 5‑ell thick wall, creating a covered passage round the solid core. Entrances lay on east and west. Only bases or stumps of many pillars remain.Ibid., p. 21 f. The core, cleared in 1904/05, is a solid square block 22 m per side and 11 m high. Naville and Winlock reconstructed it as surmounted by a pyramid, but Arnold rejects this on structural grounds.Ibid., p. 27 ff.Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, p. 159.M. Höveler‑Müller, *Am Anfang war Ägypten*, Darmstadt 2013, p. 142. === Western (rear) section === [[File:MentuhotepII.jpg|thumb|Painted limestone block from the relief programme (Naville 1907; now [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]])]] The rear portion, serving the cult of the deified king, was partly cut into the cliff and comprised an open court, a hypostyle with statue chapel, and later, a shrine to Amun‑Re, converting the complex into a true {{ill|million‑year house|de|Millionenjahrhaus|ja|ミリオネンヤールハウス|zh|百万年殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.D. Arnold, *Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep*, Bd. 1, p. 141. The middle court west of the ambulatory was flanked north and south by six columns and east by a double colonnade of eight columns. At its centre a deep [[:en:Dromos|dromos]] descends to the royal tomb. Finds include a limestone altar, a granite stele and six granite statues of [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]].Ibid., p. 33. West of the middle court lies the hypostyle hall (8 × 10 columns), separated by a wall and slightly higher.Ibid., p. 34 f. The sanctuary consists of a rock‑cut {{ill|speos|de|Speos|ja|スペオス|zh|石窟神殿|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} with a fore‑hall. All walls bore painted raised reliefs.D. Arnold, *ibid.*, Bd. 3, p. 15. Fragments show the king receiving cult as a god among gods.Ibid., p. 16. The statue room yielded an over‑life‑size standing statue of the king and a seated image of Amun‑Re, perhaps another royal theophany.Ibid., p. 33 f. === Foundation deposits === Under the terrace corners Winlock discovered intact foundation pits containing cattle skulls, food offerings, bricks and inscribed objects.Ibid., Bd. 3, p. 49 ff. Similar deposits under the core, cleared 1970, included linen inscribed with Mentuhotep’s and [[:en:Intef II|Intef II]]’s names.Ibid., Bd. 1, p. 52 ff. === The royal tomb === From the west court a 150 m sloping corridor leads to a granite burial chamber lined with rose granite and roofed corbel‑wise. Inside stood an alabaster shrine once sealed by double doors, which contained the wooden coffin and unpreserved funerary furniture of the king.Ibid., p. 44 ff.; Kühn 2010, p. 26. === Bab el‑Hosan === [[File:Bab el-Hosan.JPG|thumb|left|Entrance to Bab el‑Hosan (2010); background: Mentuhotep and Hatshepsut temples]] The Bab el‑Hosan (“Gate of the Horse”), north of the causeway, was accidentally discovered when Carter’s horse fell through its roof in 1898. It is a secondary royal tomb: a 40 m shaft and 150 m sloping corridor leading west to a chamber where Carter found the black seated statue of the king and a deeper pit containing three wooden boats and pottery.Ibid., p. 51 ff. Arnold interprets it as an Osiris tomb providing the king magical resurrection.Ibid., p. 82. === Tomb of Tem === In the southwest corner of the hypostyle lies the tomb of the great wife Tem, aligned parallel to the king’s tomb and containing a colossal alabaster sarcophagus and a fragmentary offering slab.Ibid., p. 53 f. === Six tombs of queens and a princess === [[File:ShrineOfKemsit.jpg|thumb|Chapel of Kemsit (drawing by Margaret Naville)]] [[File:MentuhotepII-ShrineOfSadhe-Entrance.JPG|thumb|Entrance to the chapel of Sadeh (after Margaret Naville)]] Six richly decorated chapels with underground shaft‑tombs for the wives [[:en:Ashayet|Ashayet]], [[:en:Sadeh (queen)|Sadeh]], [[:en:Kawit (queen)|Kawit]], [[:en:Kemsit|Kemsit]], [[:en:Henhenet|Henhenet]] and princess {{ill|Mayet|de|Majit|ja|マイト|zh|马伊特|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were set into the west wall of the ambulatory. Their identical layout suggests simultaneous death, perhaps by epidemic. Decorated sarcophagi of Ashayet and Kawit are in Cairo; Henhenet’s plain coffin is in New York.Kühn 2010, p. 23 f.D. Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975, p. 1015. === Tombs of Neferu and officials === Queen Neferu’s elaborate tomb (TT 319) was built at the north edge of the forecourt and later incorporated into Hatshepsut’s temple.Kühn 2010, p. 25. High officials were buried nearby in saff tombs aligned on the royal complex, notably those of vizier [[:en:Dagi|Dagi]] (TT 103), treasurer {{ill|Kheti|de|Cheti|ja|ヘティ|zh|赫蒂|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (TT 311) and steward [[:en:Henenu (high steward)|Henenu]] (TT 313).Kühn 2010, p. 27. == Reconstruction of the core == [[File:MentuhotepII-Tempel-Naville-rawSketch.svg|thumb|left|Naville’s reconstruction with pyramid on the core]] Naville and Winlock envisaged a 7–8 m high core topped by a pyramid, citing the [[:en:Abbott Papyrus|Abbott Papyrus]] which calls the complex a pyramid. Arnold objects that no debris of such a structure exists and the core could not bear the thrust. He proposes a stylised primeval mound with flat terrace; [[:en:Rainer Stadelmann|Rainer Stadelmann]] adds a sand‑hump planted with trees. The tomb of [[:en:Nubkheperre Intef|Nubkheperre Intef]] discovered in 2000 renewed debate: it featured a small pyramid 11 m at base. {{ill|Gunnar Sperveslage|de|Gunnar Sperveslage|ja|グンナー・スペルフェスラーゲ|zh|古纳·斯佩尔费斯拉格|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} argues analogies favour a pyramid on Mentuhotep’s core, combining Theban saff tradition with Memphite pyramid symbolism.G. Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009), p. 68. == Cult == The complexity and poor preservation limit interpretation.Arnold 1974, p. 72. Given Mentuhotep’s devotion to [[:en:Montu|Month]], much of the temple honoured Month‑Ra.Ibid., p. 75. Amun‑Ra’s cult was served by priests from [[:en:Karnak|Karnak Temple]], making this a branch sanctuary.Ibid., p. 78 ff. The goddess [[:en:Hathor|Hathor]] features prominently, implying another Hathor shrine nearby.Ibid., p. 83 f. A collegiate body of lector and purification priests tended the royal cult, while Osirian elements appear especially in Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 72 ff., 80 f. Under Mentuhotep the [[:en:Beautiful Festival of the Valley|Valley Festival]] is first attested, when Amun‑Ra’s bark visited the king’s temple.S. Schott, *Das schöne Fest vom Wüstentale*, Mainz 1953, p. 94. == History == === Construction phases === Arnold identifies four phases: A pre‑unification east forecourt wall; Phase B with massive terracing, enclosure wall and Bab el‑Hosan as original tomb; Phases C & D after the king’s Sed‑festival added ambulatory, core, middle court, rear section and abandoned Bab el‑Hosan.Ibid., p. 62 ff. === Later use === After Mentuhotep the complex was converted to an Amun‑Ra shrine. [[:en:Senusret III|Senusret III]] honoured it with granite stela and statues. New Kingdom rulers again built at Deir el‑Bahari: [[:en:Amenhotep I|Amenhotep I]] erected a small shrine; [[:en:Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]]’s great temple overshadowed Mentuhotep’s; [[:en:Thutmose III|Thutmose III]] added his own mortuary temple. Demolition began under [[:en:Ramesses IV|Ramesses IV]] or [[:en:Ramesses VI|Ramesses VI]], probably to reuse stone downstream. Removing retaining walls triggered a landslide that buried the monument.Ibid., p. 67 ff. == Literature == (chronological order) === General === * Dieter Arnold, *Der Tempel des Königs Mentuhotep von Deir el‑Bahari*, 3 vols., Mainz 1974–1981. * Dieter Arnold, “Deir el‑Bahari II,” in *Lexikon der Ägyptologie*, Bd. 1, 1975. * Dieter Arnold & Herbert E. Winlock, *The Temple of Mentuhotep at Deir el‑Bahari*, New York 1979. * Dieter Arnold, *Die Tempel Ägyptens*, Munich 1992. * {{EAAE|Rosanna Pirelli|Deir el‑Bahri, Mentuhotep II complex|239–42}} * Dieter Arnold, *Lexikon der ägyptischen Baukunst*, Düsseldorf 2000. * Thomas Kühn, “Der königliche Tempel‑ und Grabbezirk …,” *Kemet* 19/1 (2010). === Monographs (with reviews) === * Édouard Naville, *The XIth Dynasty Temple at Deir El‑Bahari*, vol. 1, London 1907. * Édouard Naville, *ibid.*, vol. 2, London 1910. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, review of Arnold vol. 1 in *Die Welt des Orients* 8 (1975/76). * Eberhard Graefe, review in *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 38 (1981). === Specific studies === * Howard Carter, “Report on the Tomb of Mentuhotep Ist …,” *ASAE* 2 (1901). * Herbert E. Winlock, *Excavations at Deir el‑Bahari 1911–1931*, New York 1942. * Ingrid Gamer‑Wallert, “Pyramiden im oberägyptischen Theben,” *Sokar* 5 (2002). * Gunnar Sperveslage, “Die Pyramide des Mentuhotep,” *Sokar* 18 (2009). == External links == {{Commonscat|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} * Mark Andrews: [http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/mentuhotept.htm The Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II on the West Bank at Luxor] * Elke Noppes: [http://www.mentuhotep.de/ Mentuhotep Nebhepetre] (in German) * Thierry Benderitter: [http://www.osirisnet.net/monument/deb/mentuhotep/deb_mentuhotep.htm Deir el Bahari. Le Temple de Mentouhotep] (in French) * [http://wysinger.homestead.com/mentuhotep.html Mentuhotep II & Wives] (homestead.com) * Theban Mapping Project: [http://www.tmpbibliography.com/resources/bibliography_4mt_mortuary_temples_a_dayr_al_bahri.html Bibliography for Dayr el‑Bahri] * Archaeowiki: {{Webarchiv|url=http://www.archaeowiki.org/Carter%27s_Description_of_the_Discovery_of_the_Bab_el-Hosan|wayback=20100829175145|text=Carter’s Description of the Discovery of the Bab el‑Hosan}} == Notes == {{Coordinate|NS=25/44/14.5/N|EW=32/36/22/E|type=landmark|region=EG-KN}} [[Category:completion tier 1]] [[Category:Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt]] [[Category:21st-century BC architecture]] [[Category:Forschungsprojekt des Deutschen Archäologischen Instituts]] [[Category:Tempel in Theben-West]] [[Category:Temples by person]] [[arz:المعبد الجنائزى لمنتوحوتب التانى]] {{Commons category|Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II}} [[en:Mortuary Temple of Mentuhotep II]] {{wikidata link|Q14551916}}[[de:Totentempel des Mentuhotep II.]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]]
